articles.title: Activision’s Halo Must Go Beyond Bungie
articles.summary: Xbox has struggled to recapture Bungie's Halo magic for 15 years. Activision's new game needs to give the series a Doom (2016) style rethink.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Matt Purslow, who was brought up on the golden era of Halo and Half-Life. He loves story-driven FPS campaigns and wishes there was more of them (but perhaps not quite as many as there were in the 2000s - that was pretty excessive.)

Of course, thanks to a $69 billion acquisition, Call of Duty is now Xbox’s Call of Duty. But I think you get the idea: Halo should be massive. It should be the premier first-person shooter on Xbox. It should be delivering stellar campaigns and phenomenal multiplayer on a regular basis. It should be among Team Green’s most-played games on any given day.

But it isn’t. And perhaps the reason why is nothing more than the passage of time and the shifting of trends. Can any game sit on the popularity throne forever? The simple truth may be that Master Chief is an artefact of the original Xbox and 360 days, and that 2010’s incredible Halo: Reach was a natural end point that should have been respected.

But while that may indeed be the case, that story doesn’t reflect Microsoft’s uneven handling of the series. Bungie delivered lightning in a bottle five times in a row over the course of a decade. Its successor, the purpose-built 343 Industries (now Halo Studios), found it all but impossible to replicate those achievements. Across 15 years, it struggled to hit a regular cadence; the development pipelines of yesteryear allowed Bungie to deliver a new game every couple of years or so, but there was a six-year gap between Halo 5 and Infinite, and very soon another six years will have passed without a mainline entry. Halo simply isn’t in the public eye in the way it was during the 360 era, nor the way Call of Duty is today.

With this in mind, it’s entirely unsurprising to see that Xbox’s CEO, Asha Sharma, has assigned Activision the task of developing the next Halo . If nothing else, Activision is an unrelenting video game factory; a colossal machine of rotating studios that assembles high-budget shooters year in, year out. If Sharma wants to ship Halo games – lots of Halo games – there’s no better Microsoft division to rectify that issue.

But cadence hasn’t been the only problem that Halo has had to contend with over the past two console generations. Simply put, there hasn’t been a must-play Halo since Bungie called it quits. The days of 90+ on Metacritic are a distant memory. That’s not to say Halo Studios’ games have been anything close to a disaster, but every one of its projects suggests a studio struggling to stay true to a formula it didn’t invent. It’s an odd situation, because (at least in theory) it followed the Bungie playbook to the letter; each of its games honors the past, maintaining traditions established way back in 2001, while also attempting to push the series into the future with brand new ideas and reworked mechanics. The Bungie era never stood still, each new game building atop its predecessor with new playable characters, new enemies, new abilities, new multiplayer modes, and even entirely new approaches to campaign design. All of this can be said of Halo Studios’ games, yet none of them ever successfully captured the magic.

Perhaps that was the biggest problem – should it have even tried to? Halo Studios was given the arguably impossible task of maintaining and continuing the legacy of one of the most important series in FPS history. Of course it tried to make games that felt like Bungie projects. But in doing so, it never successfully established a coherent new identity for the series’ next era. Halo 4 felt like a true continuation of Bungie’s work, a natural successor to the triumphs of Reach, and while I think it’s by far the best game the studio made, there’s no denying that it’s confined by pre-existing parameters and fan expectation. Halo 5 attempted to escape those rules, but its miserable campaign is the absolute worst version of something that could still be considered Halo. 2021’s Infinite was positioned as the course corrector, but turned out to be a collection of modern trends – an open world campaign, battle-pass and daily-quest-fueled multiplayer – embedded in all the iconography of a “return to roots”; the verdant green fields, blue-lit tunnels, and tight PvP arenas of Combat Evolved.

Together, the studios’ attempts make for a fractured trilogy; united by their attempts to continue the past, divided by a lack of shared direction. These troubles are only emphasised when contrasted against its Xbox stablemate, Gears of War – The Coalition’s continuation of Epic’s macho shooter similarly hasn’t lived up to the high bar of the original trilogy, but the duology of Gears 4 and 5 undeniably has its own coherent identity (which, yes, as far as the campaign goes is a bit Gears-imitating-PlayStation’s-single-player-schtick, but it’s an identity nonetheless) and that approach appears set to continue in the upcoming E-Day. Halo’s 15-year quest to stay true to Bungie has been its albatross – a lack of a truly fresh perspective dulls its edge in the modern era, while its struggle to balance the old with the new frustrates long-time Halo fans who simply want to play more Halo. It’s hard to think of another studio for which “doomed if you do, doomed if you don’t” is more applicable.

But that quest is now over. Halo Studios has been gutted, its sole reason for being handed over to the masters of Call of Duty. But while an entirely different division of Xbox may now be in charge, it faces exactly the same challenge: what is post-Bungie Halo? That question still needs an answer.

A vague, totally unsubstantiated rumour has suggested that Activision plans to totally reboot Halo. Fans are, predictably, divided by the notion . Personally, I don’t feel strongly either way, although I do think it’s time Master Chief was laid to rest. Whether the next story takes place in existing canon or not doesn’t hugely matter to me if we’re seeing the world through fresh eyes. Akin to ODST’s special forces or Reach’s team of Spartans, there’d be little need to untangle the narrative threads of John 117’s career, and the universe’s least desirable elements are easily ignored by shifting to a different theatre of war.

For me, the more important aspect is preserving the fundamental gameplay blueprint – the slower pace, the small-but-specialised arsenal, the arena approach to multiplayer, the “wide linear” campaign design, the exceptional enemy AI that makes each and every engagement unpredictable. It’s this approach that id Software took when it created its new vision of Doom – the phenomenal 2016 shooter indisputably followed the core recipe of the 1996 original, but you could never accuse it of being beholden to tradition. Every single component felt cutting-edge. It was somehow a classic, old-school shooter while simultaneously being one of the decade’s most forward-thinking games. As my colleague Ryan McCaffrey has already pointed out , it’s hard to imagine a studio better suited to handling Halo – it’s Xbox-owned, after all.

But the task has been given to Activision, and whether or not it can (or even wants to) replicate id’s success with Doom remains to be seen. But, considering the company’s history, it’s understandable if fans already have a negative outlook. Activision could well turn Halo into Xbox’s Call of Duty… by making it Call of Duty. Overstuffed menus and a relentless army of pop-ups asking you to buy the battle pass, invest in this skin, and play this limited-time mode. Halo Infinite was already showing signs of heading in that direction, so could this new era take the plunge completely and shower us with colour-tiered weapons with 16 mod slots? A battle royale map later repurposed for an extraction shooter? I wouldn’t blame anyone who’s grown tired of Call of Duty’s aggressive approach to be wary of what’s to come.

During its golden era, Bungie ensured Halo was distinct. For all its faults and failures, Halo Studios understood that – it just never managed to coalesce a coherent, compelling version of that for the series’ next generation. And so we can only hope that Activision will recognise it, too, but find more success in bringing Halo’s distinguishing qualities to a modern player base. I believe the way to do that is not to replicate the Halo of the past, but to recreate the conditions of its creation – to allow the team of designers, artists, and engineers given stewardship of the series the time and freedom to establish something as special as Combat Evolved was 25 years ago.

The reality, of course, is that Xbox cannot afford to do that. It needs a new Halo yesterday. But it also needs a damn good reason for you to buy its next-generation console. Somewhere in that pressure cooker of a situation, I hope the game that Halo’s legacy deserves can grow.

Matt Purslow is IGN's Executive Editor of Features.

articles.title: Every Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Pikachu Card, Ranked
articles.summary: There are 30 Pikachu cards in Pokémon TCG's 30th anniversary celebration set, so we've ranked them from worst to best.
articles.body:
One of the best things about Pokémon TCG’s 30th Celebration Collection is that, for the first time ever, you’re guaranteed one of these gorgeous 30 uniquely illustrated Pikachu cards in every single booster pack you open.

Each card features a distinct art style from a different legendary or rising illustrator - each style is so different and unique!

I’ve ranked all 30 of these Pikachu chase cards by artwork, using affordability as a tiebreaker based on the market median price on TCGplayer .

Keeping the hobby accessible matters now more than ever, and these cards are wonderfully affordable - with some seeing market drops of over 90% since release week.

Artwork is subjective, so to keep it fair, I averaged my own scores with four close friends from my Poké Discord who are also chasing this Pikachu master set!

Where to Buy 30th Anniversary Celebration Collection

30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection [Night]

30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection [Day]

30th Celebration Tech Sticker Collection [Lucario]

30th Celebration Battle Deck [Umbreon ex]

30th Celebration Battle Deck [Espeon ex]

30th Celebration Ditto Premium Collection

Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration - Figure Collection

Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration Binder Collection

Before we jump in, for those after 30th Celebration boosters, our best suggestion right now is to request an invite from Amazon for the ETB at least, priced much more reasonably compared to other retailers. Invites will be sent out soon! There are also preorders available for booster bundles at just $45, which is an insanely good offering!

I love Yuu Nishida as an artist! She won the first ever Pokémon Card Game Illustration Grand Prix; a contest that gives unknown artists a shot at having their work turned into a Pokémon card, and has been an Pokémon TCG official illustrator since 2019. Her pastry chef Sylveon V alternate art from Evolving Skies and the Dachsbun ex from Japan’s Stellar Miracle are two of my favorite cards of all time. This is such a classic Pikachu card, but it’s not my personal favorite Pikachu card she’s ever made - I prefer her Celebratory Fanfare Pikachu’s. Still, it’s such a baseline standard Pikachu card, it’s well worth adding to your collection.

This Pikachu card from akagi, best known for their iconic Greninja ex from Twilight Masquerade, really stands out in binders with its 3D pop. I love how the Pikachu’s look like they’re springing out the card, I’m just not personally a fan of their digital 3D models - they did something similar on their Scream Tail ex from Twilight Masquerade.

This is easily one of the most abstract pieces of art in the collection, and definitely one of the more polarizing. I appreciate a creative swing on a card, and it’s no surprise it’s the most expensive on the list for that alone. Tomokazu Komiya's cads tend to fetch a pretty penny, known for his eccentric, expressionist art style, especially on cards like Neo Discovery’s Politoed and Scarlet & Violet’s surreal Drowzee.

When you think of Naoyo Kimura and Pikachu, this isn’t the first card that comes to mind. They are the illustrator behind the infamous Van Gogh Pikachu, and it’s hard to beat that. This is a nice card, a dusky, pastel nighttime scene with a gentle Pikachu mid-step.

This card is like the evil twin of Van Gogh Pikachu, wish its brushstrokes and determined grin. Smirking directly at the viewer against a gleaming backdrop, this portrait from Nurikabe serves pure sass. I like it, because most of the other Pikachu’s in this set show off its happy demeanour more pure attitude than nearly any other card in the subset.

This high-voltage card from nagimiso reminds me of the recent Electric-type Gym leaders, with neon aesthetics. Leaping and curling through edy, abstract shapes, it reminds me of their famous Jolteon V artwork, making it a fitting style for Pokémon's premier Electric-type mascot.

Shimaris Yukichi’s artwork captures a full-cheeked Pikachu stuffing its face in a sunlit meadow, with berries scattered across a field. What really makes the composition pop is Pika’s thick, clean white outline, giving it a fun, pop-art look of an actual sticker pasted onto the card. Known for bringing cute, round Pokémon to life in charmingly simple environments, Yukichi delivers a delightfully goofy slice-of-life moment that stands out as an instant feel-good favorite.

Satoma has created a peaceful, low-key illustration of Pikachu smiling happily in a sunny flower shop. satoma, who previously drew the coveted Special Illustration Rare for Lillie's Determination brings that same soft, warm feel to this card.

Unquestionably the busiest card in the set, this card by Shinji Kanda brings their distinct pointillist art style to Pikachu. You might know them best for their iconic Magikarp card from Paldea Evolved, which has a Classic Collection reprint for the 30th Celebration. It’s no wonder that this card is the most expensive on the list.

I’ve never seen a more relaxed Pikachu; OOYAMA’s little guy is lying asleep on a tropical beach under swaying palm trees. This earned an extra point for its Ability - Tropical Vibes - which puts Pikachu to sleep in order to refresh your hand up to six cards.

Cool design, very anime-esque! There's a brilliant use of negative space within the electric sparks that makes Pikachu feel even more powerful, but overall, it just doesn’t fully grab me compared to the rest of the lineup.

Pulling off a vicious Volt Tackle, Pikachu cracks the bedrock beneath it. danciao has rapidly become one of the TCG's premier action illustrators, having drawn the Zekrom ex SIR (Black Bolt), Iron Valiant ex SIR (Prismatic Evolutions), and the widely praised Mega Charizard X ex SIR (Phantasmal Flames). This card radiates that exact same explosive, about-to-detonate energy collectors have come to expect from danciao’s high-octane portfolio!

I might catch some flack for putting the goat this low on the list, but we all agreed on this ranking! The original 1997 'Fat Pikachu' from Ken Sugimori has an unspeakable aura - this remake is lovely, but it just doesn’t hit quite the same as the iconic watercolors of the OG.

Still, it feels completely right for Game Freak's primary art director to be featured in this anniversary subset. Ken Sugimori lovingly pays homage to his classic Jungle expansion artwork here. Having illustrated well over a thousand cards dating all the way back to Base Set Blastoise, Sugimori’s inclusion beautifully bridges the gap between 1996 and today.

Pikachu leaps through a pastel dreamscape filled with floating geometry that fly past like confetti. Akira Komayama is one of the most prolific freelance artists in the TCG's history, having illustrated over 200 cards since 2010—including iconic pieces like the Chilling Reign Galarian Zapdos V alt art and Ascended Heroes’ Iono's Bellibolt ex TAG TEAM GX.

I’m a big fan of Tetsu Kayama’s textured, orange peel effect on their cards. The fun little blue sparks coming out of this Pikachu’s cheeks in a starburst pattern, with its grumpy little face, makes me really want to pick up this card.

Dangling from a thick tree branch, Rianti Hidayat’s Pikachu’s polygonal shape contrasts nicely with the curves of the leaves around it. The low-poly smile really reminds me of the N64 game Hey You, Pikachu, which doesn’t get enough attention when celebrating 30 years of Pokémon.

Pikachu is loafing on a charmingly rustic doorstep, bathing in the dappled sunlight. While Teeziro is famous for darker, dramatic masterpieces like the Evolving Skies Umbreon V, their ability to handle cinematic lighting carries over perfectly to this cozy urban scene.

For the record, I gave this card a personal 5/5! However, my "impartial" Discord judges docked points because Pikachu is so tiny that he’s technically not the focal point of the card. You decide if that’s fair or not.

Svlt’s Pikachu rests happily against a sun-warmed stone beside vibrant pink blossoms, soaking up every bit of warmth. He looks like a satisfied old man basking in the afternoon rays! Have you ever been as completely, utterly content as this Pikachu? No, me neither.

Tucked away inside a blooming bush, this Pikachu peers cautiously through bright pink flowers. Known for soft watercolor storybook scenes, Narumi Sato's naturalistic art is behind my favourite card of all time - Eevee - 188/167 from Twilight Masquerade.

This is easily the longest Pikachu I have ever seen—complete with a flat, squished face! I have three British Shorthair cats at home, and one of them absolutely loves knocking stuff off my desk while I’m trying to write. This card gives me the same energy; perched on a cluttered desk littered with open books, stationery, and office supplies, this card from Atsushi Furusawa captures a cozy, chaotic slice-of-life moment in the Pokémon world.

Amigurumi is the Japanese art of crocheting or knitting small, stuffed yarn creatures and characters. Artist Asako Ito works almost exclusively in fiber arts, meticulously stitching each doll and posing them in custom felt environments, giving this card a real tactile feel.

Lost in thought with an Ability called Lonely Gaze, this melancholic little Pikachu does something a little different from any other card on this list.

sowsow captures a quiet, bittersweet moment here, depicting Pikachu curled up on plush pillows hugging a Poké Ball cushion while staring off into the distance. It displays the exact cozy, domestic charm sowsow is known for, though there is a tragic layer if you look closely at the framed picture hanging on the wall in the background. The storytelling says so much with so little, landing at number 10 on this list.

Nuzzled deep inside a dense, mosaic-like arrangement of colorful fruit, Pikachu is rendered in thousands of intricate, pointillist dots that feel like looking at a stained-glass window up close. Illustrator Kiyotaka Oshiyama—who famously drew the fan-favorite Charizard VSTAR SWSH262 promo—brings a legendary animation pedigree to the card game. Beyond his TCG contributions, Oshiyama is an acclaimed anime director and animator, having helmed the critically lauded 2024 film Look Back and contributed key animation to powerhouse projects like Chainsaw Man and Hayao Miyazaki's The Boy and the Heron. His rare TCG appearances are always a treat, and this richly detailed Pikachu is a absolute feast for the eyes!

After winning Pokémon's 2024 Illustration Contest with a sleepy Pikachu promo and landing a Special Art Rare on Mega Rayquaza ex in Storm Emeralda, Kazuki Minami returns with an energetic, crackling Pikachu, with a washed watercolour effect you can’t help but compare to the legendary Sugimori scans. Going from contest winner to flagship anniversary contributor in two years is an incredible rise, and it’s great to support upcoming artists!

Pikachu presses his face completely flat against the glass, looking down from an open skylight with its snout squished against the window pane. Takeshi Nakamura candid, unposed style brings fantastic physical comedy to the piece, capturing a hilarious "caught in the act" perspective. Plus, I love that its move is Peer At, and he’s looking down at you while squished on a skylight.

Soaring through a neon-soaked city street at night, DOM’s urban Pika card is a steal for under a dollar. The sparks flying from it makes Pikachu look like a glowing high-speed projectile, almost like a UFO!

Peeking out from around a wooden staircase banister, with its iconic red cheeks adorably squished up against the railing, OKACHEKE has pictured Pikachu caught completely mid-sneak, looking like it got caught somewhere it definitely shouldn't be! It’s something so playful, even that high-ish price tag can't knock it from 5th place.

You can't help but fall in love with this little fella—it’s been memed endlessly across social timelines for good reason! Following the massive success of their iconic "Bubble Mew" Special Illustration Rare in Paldea Fates, artist USGMEN delivers another instant fan favorite. It’s such a simple illustration, yet it captures the feeling of seeing a friend you haven't seen in ages unexpectedly.

You don’t often see Pikachu portrayed like a feline - it is a Mouse Pokémon, after all! But here it is, lying fully tums-up in a delightfully cat-like pose. I love Susumu Maeya’s soft textures and quiet storytelling style, which give this budget card a very special feel.

I absolutely love James Turner’s creative eye - the former Game Freak Art Director (Sword & Shield) and current Creative Director at TPCi delivers one of the cleanest cards in the entire set.

Boasting bold, flat lines and zero shading, Pikachu leaps through a shower of flower petals in James Turner’s unmistakable pop-art style.

Coming in at number one has to be Pikachu’s original creator! One of the first Pokemon designers, Atsuko Nishida was brought on after Sugimori realised he had made his Pokémon designs too scary. We have her to thank for introducing the world to this electric mascot. True to reputation, this card is absolutely adorable and gets a perfect 20 in my eyes, taking the undisputed #1 crown.

Sara Heritage is a freelance journalist for IGN, specialising in Pokémon TCG. When she's not gaming, you’ll probably find her building yet another LEGO set she absolutely did not need, or chaining ranked matches in Pokémon Champions.

articles.title: Warhammer 40,000 Space Marine 2's New Class Is Finally Confirmed — and It's Exactly What Everyone Suspected
articles.summary: Big news for Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 fans today: publisher Focus Entertainment has revealed the game’s Year 3 roadmap and confirmed the new class set to hit early 2027.
articles.body:
Big news for Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 fans today: publisher Focus Entertainment has revealed the game’s Year 3 roadmap and confirmed the new class set to hit early 2027.

Let’s get straight to the headline here: the new class is — as so many had suspected — the Apothecary. In May I predicted the addition of the Apothecary as a heavy duty support class with a powerful healing ability, perhaps even with unique gameplay around harvesting Gene-seed.

“We’ve been following all your speculations ever since we teased the arrival of a new class, and you certainly had plenty of theories… and the majority of you were right!” Focus said . “Today, we’re finally revealing the truth: the Apothecary is joining the ranks with Patch 17 in the first quarter of 2027! We’ll disclose more info later, so stay tuned!

“Additionally, as we said in the previous Community Update, the Apothecary will receive a Champion skin in the same way the Techmarine did: in the update after its release.”

That’s all we have on the Apothecary, unfortunately, but we have plenty more on Year 3. Patch 15 hits October 1, with Patch 16 out before the end of this year. The long-awaited Chaos Siege mode, which lets you to play Heretic Astartes previously exclusive to PvP, arrives with Patch 15, as does the One-Handed Thunder Hammer. Patch 16 adds a brand-new PvP mode featuring Weekly Stratagems, just like in PvE.

2027 will being the Apothecary, as mentioned, new Operations and weapons, and “reworks to several gameplay features, with improvements coming to some of the game’s core systems,” Focus said.

“Additionally, there are a couple of other cool features that are planned, but not listed in the roadmap,” the publisher teased.

Focus also teased new customization features by saying it’s “something that will expand customization options by 33%,” and “something that will put our streaming tech to a test.”

Meanwhile, Year 3 DLC includes five new Cosmetic and Champion Packs, with the final one remaining redacted for now.

Developer Saber Interactive is of course working on Space Marine 3, which Tim Willits recently teased in an interview with IGN from gamescom . There’s no release window yet, but there’s a great deal of anticipation for it following the breakout success of Space Marine 2, which has seen over 12 million players since its 2024 launch.

articles.title: Reddit mod ordered to pay Nintendo $4.5 million in Switch piracy lawsuit
articles.summary: Nintendo has won a $4.5 million default judgment against Reddit moderator James Williams, who is accused of distributing pirated Switch games.
articles.body: Nintendo won its $4.5 million lawsuit against James Williams, a Reddit moderator accused of distributing pirated Switch games, as reported earlier by Aftermath. In a default judgment issued on Wednesday, a Washington federal judge also ordered Williams to shut down the online stores allegedly housing libraries of pirated Switch games. Nintendo sued Williams, also known as “archbox” online, in 2024. In its complaint, the gaming giant claimed Williams became a “leading moderator” of the r/SwitchPirates community, where he allegedly solicited “donations” of Nintendo eShop gift cards and copies of Switch games “to be copied and distributed” on online pirate stores. Last October, Nintendo asked the court for a $4.5 million default judgment after Williams didn’t respond to the lawsuit. “NOA [Nintendo of America] has demonstrated that Williams promoted online shops offering pirated Nintendo game files and circumvention software, encouraged others to contribute pirated Nintendo games to his pirate shops, and assisted others in distributing pirated Nintendo Switch games, even though he knew such activity violated copyright laws,” US District Judge Lauren King writes in the order. This marks yet another legal victory for Nintendo, which has filed a flurry of copyright lawsuits over the past several years. The company most recently won a court case in the Netherlands, which deemed it illegal to sell Mig flash cartridges that allow people to play pirated copies of games. The $4.5 million award reflects $150,000 per violation across 30 copyrighted games, including Animal Crossing: New Horizons, Luigi’s Mansion 3, and Pikmin 4. Williams must also “immediately disable access” to his alleged pirate shops, as well as shut down any social media accounts used to distribute copyrighted Switch games.

articles.title: The Xbox reset gets ugly
articles.summary: Another round of cuts leaves big questions over the future of Game Pass and the Xbox platform.
articles.body: It feels like Xbox has been in a permanent state of turmoil for at least two years now, and this week is no different. Microsoft cut 268 jobs across its gaming division this week, shuffled major studios and franchises around, and continued its Xbox “reset.” Layoffs have become a way of life for Xbox employees, after Microsoft started cutting thousands in early 2024 and hasn’t slowed down. The turmoil was particularly apparent when Microsoft started shutting down game studios, and the painful layoffs have had a lasting impact on morale, according to current and former Xbox employees I’ve been speaking to this week. At the same time, Xbox hardware is under pressure, Game Pass keeps being reshaped, and the future of Xbox as a brand feels more uncertain than ever before. This week was also a reminder that Microsoft is still very much in the middle of figuring out Xbox’s future. Nothing demonstrates the scale of change going on inside the Xbox organization than Halo. “If we lose our way with Halo, we lose our way with Xbox,” said former Xbox chief Phil Spencer in 2011. It’s been clear for years that Microsoft has lost its way with Halo, and the company has definitely lost its way with Xbox. Instead of moving the Halo Studios team under Activision directly, Microsoft is laying off most of the studio after years of layoffs, leadership changes, and technical shifts. A shell of the team is being kept in place to handle existing games like Halo Infinite and the recently shipped Halo: Combat Evolved. One source tells me that the next Halo game under Halo Studios was years away from shipping, so Microsoft pulled the plug instead. I understand that some Halo Studios employees had to wait hours to find out if they had been impacted by the layoffs earlier this week. The first communication came in a public Xbox blog, before notifications were sent to employees throughout the morning. For some, the layoffs were a relief. “I’m a jumble of thoughts and emotions, but mostly relief,” wrote former Halo Studios employee Ron B on LinkedIn. “I was miserable for the last year and a half and it’ll be nice to feel something different.” For many others, the announcement was met with anger or confusion. “Promoted and laid off in the same week is pretty wild,” said Josh Daniels, former cinematic director at Halo Studios. Shannon Loftis, who spent nearly 30 years at Microsoft working on franchises like Fable and Project Gotham Racing, didn’t hold back on criticism of Xbox chief Asha Sharma. “Super funny that Asha Sharma said ‘clarity is kindness’ to the WSJ last week then did a half layoff today,” said Loftis in a post on Threads. “I guess Damocles’ Sword is a form of clarity, what do I know?” Loftis was the former head of World’s Edge before she retired from Microsoft in 2022, the studio behind Age of Empires. The fan-focused studio is now being moved into Activision, with some layoffs impacting the team as part of this ongoing Xbox “reset.” Rare, the developers of Sea of Thieves, are also part of this latest shake-up, moving under Activision control. Forza developers Turn 10 Studios and Playground Games are also merging into a single studio, a year after Microsoft gutted Turn 10. Even Obsidian is being moved out from Xbox Game Studios and under Bethesda Game Studios, where it will work on a new entry in the Fallout franchise. Beyond the studio changes, there are also cuts to the core business planning and management areas of Xbox. “These aren’t cuts a serious business makes, in my opinion,” says video game industry analyst Mat Piscatella. Loftis was even more critical, saying “Xbox has become a business best described as ‘squandered.’ They’re [sic] squandered everything: talent, IP, time, money, gamers, community, goodwill, brand equity, stable services, profitable, knowledge.” The changes are part of Sharma’s “most significant restructure in Xbox history.” She previously told employees that she will make significant cuts to reset the Xbox content portfolio, platform, and operations. Some of the cuts feel like they could be part of a broader restructure designed to make Xbox easier to spin off, or to operate as a wholly owned subsidiary in the same way Microsoft already does with Activision and LinkedIn. Management layers are being reduced, smaller studios are being offloaded, and the focus appears to be on larger franchises and a nearly impossible goal of reaching “more than a billion people each day.” Beneath all the buzzwords in corporate memos, it’s clear that by moving these studios and franchises around, Sharma wants to get bigger games out quicker and at less cost. Microsoft has spent more than a decade acquiring and investing in studios under its Xbox Game Studios umbrella. At one point it had 15 dedicated first-party studios, but that part of the overall Xbox studios organization looks barren now. There’s a shell of Halo Studios for now, a team for Microsoft Flight Simulator, and the Xbox publishing arm, but beyond that all that’s really left is Forza Horizon developers Playground Games, Gears of War developers The Coalition, and inXile who are currently working on Clockwork Revolution. Sharma already has Minecraft developer Mojang reporting to her directly, and the rest have been shifted to Activision to presumably focus on multi-platform games. Some employees I’ve been speaking to think it’s inevitable that The Coalition and inXile will be impacted by layoffs once Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution have shipped. In fact, Microsoft already started some Coalition layoffs this week. Both studios also happen to be the ones shipping Xbox-exclusive games. If Microsoft does continue gutting Xbox Game Studios then this also speaks volumes about the platform strategy. Many of Microsoft’s core first-party Xbox studios were established to showcase Xbox hardware. The Coalition has pushed the limits of what’s possible on Xbox consoles over the years, with real expertise on Unreal Engine that has benefited other projects at Xbox. These studios have also contributed heavily to Xbox Game Pass. Microsoft has been tweaking its subscription service nonstop over the past couple of years, adding and removing Call of Duty from the service, flip-flopping on pricing, and making U-turns on cloud access. It’s clear that Game Pass isn’t quite working for Microsoft, despite previous promises that the service was profitable. I’ve heard from multiple sources over the years that there has always been a tension between Xbox leadership and studios over putting games on Xbox Game Pass. Putting a title on Game Pass cannibalizes traditional buy-to-play game sales, and the return isn’t always quantified in a boost in subscription numbers. Xbox lost $300 million in Call of Duty sales because of its addition to Game Pass, prompting Microsoft to quickly reverse course on bringing new entries in the franchise to the service. With fewer first-party studios making day-one games for Game Pass, it seems inevitable that Microsoft will tweak the Game Pass formula again. Rumors suggest that Microsoft is working on an overhaul to Game Pass that will create tiers with or without ads, much like Netflix and other streaming services. These new tiers will reportedly debut without access to day-one games, as well as add-on bundles for cloud gaming and a new family plan option. Microsoft has already pulled day-one games for its Game Pass Premium subscription, so I wouldn’t be surprised to see more changes ahead. Significant changes to Game Pass could also reflect the reality of the Xbox hardware situation. Sources at Xbox tell me that Grand Theft Auto VI preorders are heavily skewed toward PS5, ringing yet more alarm bells about the platform. Xbox hardware revenue has now declined for three straight years, and RAMageddon is pushing the prices of Xbox Series X consoles higher and higher. It’s getting increasingly harder to predict what this all means for Project Helix, Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console. As you can probably tell, piecing together Microsoft’s Xbox strategy is challenging. One thing is clear, though: The cuts aren’t over yet. Microsoft says it’s roughly three-quarters of the way through its Xbox restructuring, leaving employees with the prospect of more upheaval hanging over them for the foreseeable future. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: Even as Absolute Batgirl Finally Appears, Absolute Batman #24 Succeeds By Keeping the Focus on Bruce Wayne and Scarecrow
articles.summary: With the debut of Absolute Batgirl, Absolute Batman #24 almost has too much going on, but the series succeeds by keeping the focus mostly on Batman himself.
articles.body:
To hear them tell it, Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta still have years' worth of stories they want to tell on Absolute Batman . But you almost wouldn't know it from reading the series' current story arc. "The Straw Man" is so crammed full of new characters and key plot twists that it almost feels like the creators are trying to leave it all out on the floor before bidding readers farewell. At times, this arc has threatened to crumble under its own massive weight, but issue #24 is able to keep all those plates spinning while adding in yet another key Bat-character for good measure.

The big news with Absolute Batman #24 is the debut of Absolute Batgirl. Dragotta even pays a lovely tribute to the now-iconic cover of issue #1 with his latest cover image:

Readers should keep their expectations in check as far as Batgirl's role in this issue is concerned, however. She's more a secondary element rather than the main focus of the issue. Mostly, it's just nice to see the series establishing a new heroine and putting a win in Bruce's column after bombarding him with pain and misery for the entirety of this story arc.

That really gets to the heart of Absolute Batman #24's appeal. There's been so much darkness fueling the series of late, from the apparent but not actual death of Martha Wayne to Batman being framed for multiple murders to Bruce being hit with the realization that his entire existence may have been orchestrated by the Joker. This deep into "The Straw Man," it's really vital that the series give readers (and Bruce himself) reason to feel hope. Absolute Batman has been so adept at transforming Scarecrow into a metaphor for our current age of fear and paranoia, but we need to be reminded that good still has a chance of triumphing over fear and despair, even in this twisted universe.

Accordingly, issue #24 is great about exploring Bruce at his lowest ebb and forcing him back into the light. All of the secondary characters and plot threads - Deathstroke and the Robins, Bruce's former friends-turned-villains, etc. - take a backseat to the core tale of Batman getting his Bat-groove back. We're treated to a very satisfying showdown between Bats and Scarecrow, as the series finally acknolwedges that there are limits even to the latter's unnatural power.

Absolute Batman Vol. 1: The Zoo (Hardcover)

Mind you, this is still a very densely packed story, with many supporting characters and the series continuing to emphasize multiple parallel time periods and points of view. As ever, this series only works when the creative team are fully in sync with one another. Dragotta is adept at taking Snyder's complex script and making it digestible on the page. It's never hard to follow the script, even as it bounces between locations and time periods. It helps that Frank Martin's colors draw such a clear distinction between past and present.

Issue #24 is also a terrific showcase for Dragotta's character designs. I love the visual approach to Two-Face here and how Dragotta makes use of the character's long hair and manga-inspired appearance. The Batgirl design is also a very different, very satisfying overhaul to a familiar character. But best of all this month is Scarecrow himself, as we see just how distorted and inhuman this villain can become. Thanks in no small part to Dragotta's art, this character is terrifying in a way he rarely is in other Batman comics.

Unfortunately, as dense as this issue is with plot points, some elements are inevitably going to feel shortchanged. The flashback storyline is the main victim in Absolute Batman #24. The saga of Bruce's short-lived tenure as a mob enforcer reaches a critical point here, and while it mirrors the main storyline nicely, it would have been great to see this plot thread play out in greater depth. That's especially felt once it becomes clear that Snyder and Dragotta are putting their own spin on one of the most iconic Batman moments of all time.

articles.title: The $1,299 Meta VR Glasses Prove That High Prices Are the New Normal
articles.summary: Meta finally announced its long-rumored Meta VR Glasses last night at Connect, and while they seem like a cool little gadget, they're coming in at a $1,299 asking price – the same that Valve is charging for its 1TB Steam Frame. The difference, though, is that Meta's headset has less RAM and storage, even if it comes in a flashy new form factor.
articles.body:
Meta finally announced its long-rumored Meta VR Glasses last night at Connect . While they seem like a cool little gadget, they're coming in at a $1,299 asking price – the same that Valve is charging for its 1TB Steam Frame. The difference, though, is that Meta's headset has less RAM and storage, even if it comes in a flashy new form factor.

The Meta VR Glasses do all of their processing through a 'computing puck' that you keep in your pocket, according to Engadget . That puck includes 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, which is paired with Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite chip. That chip is built for VR and XR, and is probably going to be faster than the aging Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 found in the Steam Frame , but I don't think it's so much better that it's worth the tradeoff of less RAM and such a tiny drive.

A lot of the price of the Meta VR Glasses probably comes down to engineering a VR headset that weighs just 100g on your head – again, that's not including the 'computing puck' – but it's a stark increase over the Meta Quest 3 that preceded it. What's more, unlike something like the Steam Frame, Meta is likely going to aggressively push extra subscriptions and add-ons to unlock the full potential of the device — and that's not to mention all the data you're likely signing away when you set the thing up.

Those extra services and data harvesting should mean a more affordable device. For all we know, it might be cheaper than it would be without it, but it's just another sign that the ongoing RAM crisis is raising the price on all kinds of devices. It's hard to say how much this headset would have cost before RAM and storage went through the roof, but at least for the latter, the high prices are probably why Meta went with 128GB of storage instead of the 512GB that comes with the Meta Quest 3. Luckily, the puck does have an microSD card reader.

Back when I reviewed the Steam Frame, I kept looking at the Meta Quest 3 as this kind of golden ideal of how much a VR headset should cost, even though it's clear that Meta has defied gravity by avoiding raising the price on it so far.

The Meta VR Glasses do have more of a professional sheen to them than something like the Quest 3 ever did, but the company still spent a huge amount of time on stage talking about them like they're a "private theater screen." To be fair, that's absolutely how I would use them, but at $1,299, you start getting to the point where you can buy a pretty nice TV for far less money.

At the end of the day, if there was any company I'd expect to use software sales and data harvesting to subsidize VR hardware, it'd be Meta. And if these VR Glasses are coming in at $1,299 this spring, it's hard to imagine that any upcoming hardware is going to very affordable.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

Check out the trailer for V/H/S/MIXTAPE, an upcoming horror film featuring new segments from directors Ernest Dickerson, Flying Lotus, Tobias Forge, David Moreau, RZA, and Renee Zhan. The latest installment pushes the boundaries of found footage with four wildly original stories that each put a unique spin on the terrifying relationship between sound and fear. V/HS/MIXTAPE features GWAR and Jim Henson's Creature Shop. V/H/S/MIXTAPE cranks the franchise's signature found-footage horror up to eleven with an electrifying new anthology where music and sound become the source of terror. United by a theme that explores the power of music, rhythm, and audio to haunt, possess, transform, and destroy, the film blends cosmic horror, psychological suspense, outrageous splatter, and groundbreaking practical effects into one unforgettable mixtape of nightmares.V/H/S/MIXTAPE is produced by Josh Goldbloom, Steven Schneider, Roy Lee, Michael Schreiber, and Brad Miska. Ben Ross and Rami Yasin serve as executive producers. It is written by Zoe Cooper, David Moreau, Ernest Dickerson, RZA, and Matt Landsman.

V/H/S/MIXTAPE streams on Shudder beginning October 9, 2026.

articles.title: Strange New Worlds Ends a Frustrating Season on a High Note With a Uhura Time-Travel Story
articles.summary: Strange New Worlds ends a frustrating season on a high note, with a Uhura time-travel story that helps to wash away some of the memories of the high-concept episodes that have preceded it.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 10, “Tomorrow’s Enterprise.”

Putting aside the promise of a title like “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” – which obviously echoes the all-time-great Next Gen episode “Yesterday’s Enterprise – as well as any fan hopes for a Captain Seven from Star Trek: Picard showing up with the crew of the Enterprise-G (yes, some folks were holding out for that unlikely team-up), the Season 4 finale of Strange New Worlds is an enjoyable finish to an incredibly frustrating 10-episode run of highs and lows.

Zeroing in on Celia Rose Gooding’s Nyota Uhura, “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” is time-travel romp that also functions as a sort of preview of this iteration of the USS Enterprise crew’s end – as well as the show’s. While investigating a white hole – “a unique and rare occurrence,” as Uhura says in her log – as well as fending off Scotty (Martin Quinn), who wants to ask his crewmate out on a date, the newly promoted lieutenant takes a hit to the noggin after the phenomenon unexpectedly erupts with energy. Next thing she knows, she’s hearing Scotty over the comms suffering some kind of deadly accident… but nobody else hears it or believes her. Nobody except… her future self!

Uhura has often proved to be a great lens through which to tell Strange New Worlds stories, first as the young cadet who was just learning the ropes of serving on a starship, all the way through discovering the hard truths of the job (Hemmer, we miss you!) and the sublime moments it can also offer. And Rose Gooding is terrific as always in this week’s episode as she has to play not just the current-day Uhura, but also the Uhura she’ll be in a year’s time.

Speaking of which, Akiva Goldsman and Henry Alonso Myers, the showrunners of Strange New Worlds, have never tried to hide how much they want to tell stories with The Original Series crew – they were planning a spin-off of SNW called Star Trek: Year One, after all. So once again we get a version of the Enterprise where Kirk is now captain. The events of this future timeline are slightly off, since Scotty is dead after the accident that happens in the past, but you gotta figure it’s mostly correct? I think? If you’re willing to take that leap, then we know Pike has less than a year left before he becomes an admiral and Kirk takes over, Ortegas (Melissa Navia) is going to leave the ship to become a flight instructor, and La’An… well, she’s not around anymore, but nobody wants to talk about it. It’s all a tantalizing tease for how Strange New Worlds might end.

As for the romance between Uhura and Scotty that’s happening in the future timeline, it’s also funny how this show keeps going back to the Star Trek V: The Final Frontier well. And I’m here for it! That movie – which used to be considered one of the worst of the original crew’s films, though I think that take has softened over the decades (I love it, flaws and all) – did allude to a romantic relationship between the two characters, but it never went beyond that. And really, it’s never made sense that the crews of these starships aren’t hooking up more. Plus, Rose Gooding and Quinn have plenty of chemistry and charisma. Here’s hoping Strange New Worlds keeps pushing this particular final frontier next season.

The problem “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” faces is how everything is wrapped up, however, with the white hole (and black hole on the other side of it in the future timeline) turning out to be some kind of space baby-producing galactic phenomenon that we can’t hope to truly understand… but which tidies up all the problems Uhura has faced for the past hour in a deus ex machina that really puts the deus in the machina .

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

Scotty checking his breath before he talks Uhura. You know you’ve been there!

Uhura pretending to not hear Scotty ask her out. You know you’ve been there!

Aha, a Gary Mitchell reference! I just was wondering a couple of weeks ago what happened to Jenna Mitchell (Rong Fu), who was often at the helm of the Enterprise in previous seasons. But also, it was always weird to have a Mitchell sitting there since we knew that Gary Mitchell would eventually take that position – the Gary Lockwood character who was Kirk’s best friend and turned into a god-like being in the first William Shatner episode of TOS, “Where No Man Has Gone Before.” Now we know Jenna and Gary are step-siblings… and have the same job, I guess?

Bones also gets a mention here, as he apparently serves as a medical officer alongside Dr. Boyce in the future timeline while Dr. M’Benga is off on Vulcan. This lines up with M’Benga eventually being a Vulcan expert on TOS, but it still doesn’t account for where Dr. Mark Piper is (the doctor in that same first episode with Shatner).

Man, the Enterprise has suddenly got all kinds of aliens walking around. I spotted a member of the cat-like species, the Caitians (M’Ress in live-action!?), a bird-like Aurelian, some kind of reptilian dude who was hanging out with a shirt on but no pants like Donald Duck, and some others too. Who was your favorite?

articles.title: Call of Duty: Warzone Is Getting a New Toggle That Lets You Turn Off All Those Goofy Skins
articles.summary: Call of Duty: Warzone is getting a new Operator Skin toggle, which means you can finally turn off all those goofy skins.
articles.body:
Call of Duty: Warzone is getting a new Operator Skin toggle, which means you can finally turn off all those goofy skins.

Activision said that from Season 1 of the upcoming Modern Warfare 4 , this new Operator Skin toggle will be available to let players see only Modern Warfare 4 Operators in the game.

When the toggle is on, you see a Modern Warfare 4 Operator in place of any Operator or Operator Skin from another Call of Duty game that's been equipped by another player. This applies to enemies, party members, and squadmates, both in the lobby and during a match, Activision said in a blog post .

Your own equipped Operator won’t change, so you’ll continue to see the Operator you selected, even if it’s from another game. The toggle only impacts your game, not the experience of others, and will be OFF by default.

Operators and Weapons from Modern Warfare 2, Modern Warfare 3, Black Ops 6, and Black Ops 7 will remain available in Warzone starting with Season 1, including the Skins, Blueprints, and Camos you’ve earned and bought for them. “The collection you’ve built remains yours to use, and existing plans for Carry Forward for previous titles are not affected with this update,” Activision said.

“Over the last few years, Call of Duty: Warzone has brought together Operators, weapons, and experiences from across recent Call of Duty titles in one shared experience,” Activision continued. “We know some players enjoy that variety, while others would prefer Call of Duty: Warzone feel more aligned with the world of the latest release, including the upcoming Modern Warfare 4.

This is big news for Call of Duty fans, many of whom had complained about goofy skins particularly in Black Ops 6. With the likes of Beavis and Butt-Head and American Dad hitting Black Ops 6 shortly after weed-obsessed bundles starring Seth Rogen, some fans said they’d had enough of what they called the 'Fortnite-ification' of their beloved Call of Duty, and pleaded with publisher Activision to return to its mil-sim roots. Those complaints sparked a U-turn at Activision for last year's Black Ops 7, amid pressure from rival shooter Battlefield 6 and its commitment to “gritty realism.”

In May, Infinity Ward told fans to "keep the receipts" after promising to remain grounded regarding cosmetics in Modern Warfare 4.

But why not add this toggle in Black Ops 6? In a social media post , Activision insisted the toggle "required new tech that will only be available starting with Season 01."

Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 and Warzone's Bloke Biter Shark Skin Screenshots

Back with Warzone, Activision said all weapons from Modern Warfare 2 through Black Ops 7 will continue to be accessible through the Legacy tab in the Loadout menu of Call of Duty: Warzone. While these Weapons remain available to use, Gunsmith functionality and prior Custom Loadouts will not be supported for legacy Weapons or legacy Blueprints. However, these won’t be left as base Weapons without Attachments; instead a five-attachment version of each legacy base Weapon will be available, as well as any Blueprint for a legacy Weapon with their existing Attachment setups.

“Our goal for this chapter of Call of Duty: Warzone is for the weapon meta to feel distinctly rooted in Modern Warfare 4, while preserving access to nostalgic choices that players know and love,” Activision said. “Raven Software will continue to deliver on its commitment to balancing weapons on a biweekly basis, keeping the MW4 weapon lineup fluid and interesting throughout each season.”
